title: Structured Neural SDEs for Functional Calibration

paper.title: Structured Neural SDEs for Functional Calibration
paper.abstract:
Abstract Neural Stochastic Differential Equations (Neural SDEs) provide flexible
continuous-time generative models, but generic neural drift and diffusion
networks are costly to simulate on long horizons and can give unstable
gradients when the training signal is a path functional rather than a
pointwise observation. We introduce SLiSDE , a family of Neural SDE
models built from structured linear stochastic layers. Parallel-in-time
simulation is obtained at the layer level, while expressivity is recovered
by gated in-flow stacking: previous-layer paths modulate the next
layer’s latent flow through learned gates. For
functional calibration tasks in which rare paths dominate the loss, we add
an optional Girsanov tilt
that acts as a learned importance
sampler with an exact likelihood-ratio correction. We prove
well-posedness, a discretisation error bound, validity of the change of
measure, and a universality result: the terminal laws of the gated stack
are dense in the space of square-integrable laws. Experiments on
functional calibration benchmarks show that the structured model
outperforms fully neural SDE baselines while retaining parallel-time
simulation and stable importance weights.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Many quantities of practical interest are expectations of functionals of a stochastic path whose trajectories are never observed. In derivatives markets the available data are option quotes – expectations of terminal payoffs – and exceedance probabilities, and calibrating a model of the underlying dynamics to such quotes is the entry point of pricing, hedging and risk management ( Buehler et al., 2019 ) ; the same situation, dynamics observed only through a finite family of statistics, arises in the physical sciences. We refer to this task as functional calibration : fitting a generative model of continuous-time stochastic dynamics to prescribed expectations of path functionals. Training such a model requires simulating it afresh at every gradient step, so the computational cost of simulation is the binding constraint, and it is the constraint that shapes the model proposed here. Neural differential equations provide a flexible framework for learning continuous-time dynamics by parameterizing their vector fields with neural networks. Neural ODEs ( Chen et al., 2018 ) model deterministic latent evolution, neural CDEs ( Kidger et al., 2020 ; Walker et al., 2025 ) condition the dynamics on an observed driving path, and neural SDEs ( Tzen and Raginsky, 2019 ) provide the stochastic analogue, modeling distributions on continuous-time paths via stochastic differential equations, which may be interpreted in either the Itô or Stratonovich sense. In this work, we focus on the Itô setting, where the latent state evolves as d ​ Z t = μ θ ​ ( t , Z t ) ​ d ​ t + σ θ ​ ( t , Z t ) ​ d ​ W t , Z 0 ∼ p 0 , \,\mathrm{d}Z_{t}=\mu_{\theta}(t,Z_{t})\,\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{\theta}(t,Z_{t})\,\,\mathrm{d}W_{t},\qquad Z_{0}\sim p_{0}, (1) where W t W_{t} is a Brownian motion and μ θ \mu_{\theta} , σ θ \sigma_{\theta} unconstrained neural networks. This is a rich model class ( Tzen and Raginsky, 2019 ; Liu et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2020 ; Kidger et al., 2021 ) , and in practice it is often used as a Markovian lift : the latent state is lifted to a higher-dimensional space in which a non-Markovian observed process can be represented as a Markov diffusion. The viewpoint is powerful, but it makes simulation expensive — every time step requires fresh nonlinear evaluations of the lifted vector field, and the recurrence is inherently sequential unless additional structure is imposed. The central design principle of this paper is to move the non-linear part of the model from the non-linear drift and diffusion evaluated at every time step to non-linear coupling between structured linear SDE layers. After discretisation, each layer is an affine recurrence whose composition is associative, so it can be evaluated by the parallel associative scan of Section 2.1 , which cuts the sequential simulation cost over a horizon of T T time steps from O ⁡ ( T ) O(T) to O ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) O(\log T) . To recover expressivity, we stack such layers through gated in-flow coupling: the previous-layer path modulates the next layer’s transition and offset through learned gates. The current layer remains affine in its own state, so the scan structure is preserved, while the gates make the stack a genuinely nonlinear model, universal at the level of terminal laws (Theorem 5.3 ). For high-variance path-dependent objectives, we add an optional last-layer-only Girsanov tilt. A learned adapted controller changes only the Brownian increments driving the final layer and returns the corresponding Radon–Nikodym log-weight in closed form.

sections.heading: Related work.
sections.text: Within the neural-SDE literature two training paradigms coexist. Generative training matches the law of the model to an empirical distribution of paths through a statistical divergence – the KL divergence of variational inference ( Tzen and Raginsky, 2019 ; Li et al., 2020 ) , the Wasserstein-1 distance of the GAN formulation ( Kidger et al., 2021 ) , or signature-kernel scores ( Issa et al., 2023 ) – and requires sample paths. Calibration training, our setting, instead matches prescribed expectations of functionals, typically derivative prices, when no trajectory is observed ( Gierjatowicz et al., 2020 ; Cuchiero et al., 2020 ; Cohen et al., 2021 ) ; before neural SDEs this task was handled by parametric families that hard-wire the dynamics, such as stochastic-volatility and local-volatility models in finance or mechanistic diffusion models in the physical sciences. Structured state-space models have shown that carefully parameterised linear recurrences can achieve strong sequence-modelling performance while remaining hardware efficient ( Gu et al., 2022 ; Smith et al., 2023 ; Hasani et al., 2022 ; Gu and Dao, 2023 ) . Recent work also connects this line of models to controlled differential equations, viewing sequence transformations as dynamics driven by an input path ( Muca Cirone et al., 2024 ) . SLiCE ( Walker et al., 2025 ) develops this perspective for structured linear controlled differential equations, showing how scan-compatible linear dynamics can be embedded in a CDE-style framework. The Girsanov component is connected to importance sampling for diffusion processes and to the stochastic-control view of variance reduction ( Hartmann et al., 2017 ; Zhang and Chen, 2022 ; Hartmann and Richter, 2024 ) . In those approaches, one learns or designs a drift change that makes rare paths less rare and then corrects the resulting bias with a likelihood ratio. Our tilt is narrower: it acts only on the Brownian motion of the last SLiSDE layer. This keeps the prefix computation unchanged, and makes the proposal lightweight enough to train jointly with the backbone.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: • Structured linear neural SDE for functional calibration. We introduce a structured linear Neural SDE backbone whose discretized layers are affine recurrences. This gives O ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) O(\log T) parallel depth in sequence length by the parallel associative scan, compared with the O ⁡ ( T ) O(T) complexity of standard neural SDE solvers. • Gated in-flow stacking. We propose a gated in-flow stacking rule in which previous-layer paths modulate the next layer’s affine transition and offset. Nonlinearity enters between layers only, so each layer stays affine in its own state and scan-compatible. • Girsanov overlay. We add an optional last-layer-only Girsanov tilt with a closed-form likelihood-ratio correction: a learned adapted controller acts as a self-normalised importance sampler that improves performance on rare-event functional calibration with little added compute. • Theory. We prove that the terminal laws generated by the gated stack are dense in 𝒫 2 ​ ( ℝ p ) \mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{p}) for the 2 2 -Wasserstein distance (Theorem 5.3 ), so the structural restrictions cost nothing at the level of terminal laws. • Experiments. We evaluate the model on nonlinear path-functional calibration tasks and real option-surface benchmarks, comparing against neural SDE and structured sequence-model baselines. SLiSDE attains the lowest or a statistically tied calibration loss on every benchmark, and trains faster than SLiCE in every setting tested and faster than the Neural SDE in all but two of them; a controlled study shows the tilt as a learned importance sampler for rare-event functionals.

sections.heading: 2 Mathematical Background
sections.text: Let ( Ω , ℱ , { ℱ t } t ∈ [ 0 , T ] , ℙ ) (\Omega,\mathcal{F},\{\mathcal{F}_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]},\mathbb{P}) be a filtered probability space supporting an m m -dimensional Brownian motion W t = ( W t 1 , … , W t m ) W_{t}=(W_{t}^{1},\dots,W_{t}^{m}) on [ 0 , T ] [0,T] . We consider a time grid 0 = t 0 < t 1 < ⋯ < t N = T 0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{N}=T , with Brownian increments Δ ​ W k = W t k + 1 − W t k ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , Δ ​ t k ​ I m ) \Delta W_{k}=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_{k}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Delta t_{k}I_{m}) . Throughout, complexities are stated in terms of the horizon T T , which for a fixed step size is proportional to the number of steps N N . The Girsanov change of measure on which the tilt of Section 4 rests is recalled in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: 2.1 Linear SDEs and affine flows
sections.text: A general affine linear SDE takes the form d ​ Z t = ( A ​ Z t + b ) ​ d ​ t + ∑ j = 1 m C j ​ Z t ​ d ​ W t j + D ​ d ​ W t , Z 0 = z 0 \,\mathrm{d}Z_{t}=(AZ_{t}+b)\,\,\mathrm{d}t+\sum_{j=1}^{m}C^{j}Z_{t}\,\,\mathrm{d}W_{t}^{j}+D\,\,\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad Z_{0}=z_{0} (2) with z 0 ∈ L 2 ​ ( Ω , ℱ 0 , ℙ , ℝ d ) z_{0}\in L^{2}(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_{0},\mathbb{P};\mathbb{R}^{d}) , A , C j ∈ ℝ d × d A,C^{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} , b ∈ ℝ d b\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , and D ∈ ℝ d × m D\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m} . On each grid interval [ t k , t k + 1 ] [t_{k},t_{k+1}] its discretisation, by the matrix-exponential transition or by the Euler–Maruyama transition (Appendix C.1 ; the latter is used throughout our experiments), is an affine recurrence Z k + 1 = F k ​ Z k + g k , Z_{k+1}=F_{k}Z_{k}+g_{k}, (3) where the transition matrix F k ∈ ℝ d × d F_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and the offset g k ∈ ℝ d g_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are built from the coefficients and the Brownian increment Δ ​ W k \Delta W_{k} .

sections.heading: Parallel associative scan.
sections.text: The solution of the affine recurrence Eq. 3 can be written Z k = F ^ k ​ Z 0 + g ^ k Z_{k}=\widehat{F}_{k}Z_{0}+\widehat{g}_{k} with ( F ^ k , g ^ k ) = ( F k − 1 , g k − 1 ) ∘ ⋯ ∘ ( F 0 , g 0 ) (\widehat{F}_{k},\widehat{g}_{k})=(F_{k-1},g_{k-1})\circ\cdots\circ(F_{0},g_{0}) , where ( F ′ , g ′ ) ∘ ( F , g ) := ( F ′ ​ F , F ′ ​ g + g ′ ) (F^{\prime},g^{\prime})\circ(F,g):=(F^{\prime}F,\;F^{\prime}g+g^{\prime}) (4) is composition of affine maps. This operation is associative, so all prefixes ( F ^ k , g ^ k ) k ≤ N (\widehat{F}_{k},\widehat{g}_{k})_{k\leq N} can be computed with any bracketing, in particular along a balanced binary tree of depth O ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) O(\log T) , and the result equals the sequential recursion exactly (Proposition B.1 ). We call this evaluation the parallel associative scan and say that a recurrence is scan-compatible when its one-step maps are affine in the state; this is the only name used for the scan in the sequel. Remark 2.1 . The scan does not reduce the total arithmetic work across all time steps, but it reduces the sequential dependence from O ⁡ ( T ) O(T) recurrent updates to O ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) O(\log T) parallel depth, exposing the time dimension to parallel hardware.

sections.heading: 2.2 Functional calibration objective
sections.text: Let Y θ Y^{\theta} denote the output path of a model with parameters θ \theta . The data of a functional calibration problem are a finite family Φ \Phi of path functionals φ \varphi , each with a prescribed value c φ c_{\varphi} of its expectation; no trajectory is observed. Given n n independent model paths Y θ , 1 , … , Y θ , n Y^{\theta,1},\dots,Y^{\theta,n} and the Monte-Carlo average 𝔼 ^ θ , n ​ [ φ ] = n − 1 ​ ∑ i = 1 n φ ⁡ ( Y θ , i ) \widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{\theta,n}[\varphi]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varphi(Y^{\theta,i}) , the objective is ℒ n ​ ( θ ) = ∑ φ ∈ Φ w φ ​ ( 𝔼 ^ θ , n ​ [ φ ] − c φ ) 2 , w φ > 0 , \mathcal{L}_{n}(\theta)=\sum_{\varphi\in\Phi}w_{\varphi}\Bigl(\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{\theta,n}[\varphi]-c_{\varphi}\Bigr)^{2},\qquad w_{\varphi}>0, (5) minimised by stochastic gradient descent with a fresh sample of n n paths at every step. In this context no model path is paired with a data path: Eq. 5 is a functional of the model law rather than a samplewise error. Since 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( 𝔼 ^ θ , n ​ [ φ ] − c φ ) 2 ] = ( 𝔼 θ ​ [ φ ] − c φ ) 2 + n − 1 ​ Var θ ⁡ ( φ ) \mathbb{E}[(\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{\theta,n}[\varphi]-c_{\varphi})^{2}]=(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\varphi]-c_{\varphi})^{2}+n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}_{\theta}(\varphi) , it converges almost surely to the population objective ℒ ∞ ​ ( θ ) = ∑ φ w φ ​ ( 𝔼 θ ​ [ φ ] − c φ ) 2 \mathcal{L}_{\infty}(\theta)=\sum_{\varphi}w_{\varphi}(\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\varphi]-c_{\varphi})^{2} , the Monte-Carlo variance entering at order 1 / n 1/n only, so there is no incentive to collapse the model law onto a mean. Finitely many expectation constraints do not determine the path law, and ℒ ∞ \mathcal{L}_{\infty} has no unique minimiser; this is a property of the task rather than of the objective, and the selected model is validated on functionals it was never fitted to. Where a reference dynamics is available, a relative-entropy penalty turns Eq. 5 into a selection rule that drops into the training loop unchanged. Appendix A.2 develops these points and relates the objective to divergence-based generative training.

sections.heading: 3 The SLiSDE Model
sections.text: A SLiSDE is built by composing structured linear stochastic layers through a stacking mechanism, followed by a learned linear readout. The optional Girsanov component is described separately in Section 4 .

sections.heading: 3.1 Structured linear base layer
sections.text: For latent dimension d d and Brownian dimension m m , each structured layer is an Itô SDE of the form d ​ Z t = ( A t ​ Z t + b t ) ​ d ​ t + ∑ j = 1 m ( C t j ​ Z t + d t j ) ​ d ​ W t j , Z 0 = z 0 , \,\mathrm{d}Z_{t}=\big(A_{t}Z_{t}+b_{t}\big)\,\,\mathrm{d}t+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\big(C_{t}^{j}Z_{t}+d_{t}^{j}\big)\,\,\mathrm{d}W_{t}^{j},\quad Z_{0}=z_{0}, (6) where A t , C t j ∈ ℝ d × d A_{t},C_{t}^{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and b t , d t j ∈ ℝ d b_{t},d_{t}^{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and we assume that z 0 ∈ L 2 ​ ( Ω , ℱ 0 , ℙ , ℝ d ) z_{0}\in L^{2}(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_{0},\mathbb{P};\mathbb{R}^{d}) . Under coefficient bounds that hold by construction (Appendix B.1 ), the layer has a unique strong solution with moment bounds independent of the time grid (Theorem 5.1 ). We write ( A t , b t , C t 1 , … , C t m , d t 1 , … , d t m ) (A_{t},b_{t},C_{t}^{1},\ldots,C_{t}^{m},d_{t}^{1},\ldots,d_{t}^{m}) for the time-indexed coefficient family induced by the model parameters. These parameters contain static structured coefficients ( A , b , C 1 , … , C m , d 1 , … , d m ) ∈ Θ (A,b,C^{1},\ldots,C^{m},d^{1},\ldots,d^{m})\in\Theta , where Θ \Theta denotes the set of trainable weights, together with optional time-feature decoder weights. The matrices A A and C j C^{j} are chosen from a fixed structured family: diagonal , block-diagonal , or dense . The additive diffusion vectors d j d^{j} may be (jointly) represented densely or through a low-rank parameterisation. Remark 3.1 (Time-dependent coefficients) . The map A ↦ A t A\mapsto A_{t} , and similarly for b , C j , d j b,C^{j},d^{j} , is optional and makes the coefficients time dependent through a small deterministic time-feature decoder (described in Appendix C.2 ). In both cases the layer remains linear in the current state Z t Z_{t} . Remark 3.2 (Noise type) . The noise type may be controlled by switching off parts of the diffusion. If d t j = 0 d_{t}^{j}=0 for all j j , the layer has only multiplicative noise; if C t j = 0 C_{t}^{j}=0 for all j j , the layer has only additive noise; and if both terms are retained, the layer has general affine diffusion. After discretisation, the layer produces affine transition pairs ( F k , g k ) (F_{k},g_{k}) of the form of Eq. 3 , with the static coefficients of the transitions of Appendix C.1 replaced by their time-dependent values at t k t_{k} . The choice of matrix structure is important computationally: diagonal, block-diagonal, and dense matrices are closed under matrix multiplication, so products of transition matrices remain in the same family. This closure is what allows the affine maps to be composed by the parallel associative scan with O ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) O(\log T) parallel depth without leaving the chosen representation. By contrast, other cheap matrix parameterization families such as fixed-rank low-rank or DPLR matrices do not satisfy this property, thus requiring sequential recursion and O ⁡ ( T ) O(T) complexity.

sections.heading: 3.2 Residual stacking (sequence-model baseline)
sections.text: Sequence models such as Mamba ( Gu and Dao, 2023 ) and the linear CDE SLiCE ( Walker et al., 2025 ) build depth by residual stacking : a sequence block 𝒮 ( ℓ ) \mathcal{S}^{(\ell)} is applied to a normalised hidden path and added back, H ( ℓ ) = H ( ℓ − 1 ) + 𝒮 ( ℓ ) ​ ( Norm ⁡ ( H ( ℓ − 1 ) ) ) H^{(\ell)}=H^{(\ell-1)}+\mathcal{S}^{(\ell)}(\operatorname{Norm}(H^{(\ell-1)})) , so a single hidden path is refined layer by layer. This is the natural depth mechanism to compare against. It is, however, ill-suited to our setting: each SLiSDE layer is itself a Brownian-driven SDE, so reusing the previous layer’s already-Brownian path as the driver of the next would turn that layer into a deterministic transform of an already-stochastic input, adding compositional depth but injecting no fresh randomness per layer. We therefore do not stack SLiSDE layers residually; instead we couple them through the flow itself, via gated in-flow stacking (Section 3.3 ).

sections.heading: 3.3 Gated in-flow stacking
sections.text: Our main architectural contribution is gated in-flow stacking : a selective, path-dependent modulation of the next layer’s affine flow, in the spirit of selective state-space models but adapted to stochastic latent dynamics. Layer ℓ \ell builds its affine transition pairs ( F k ( ℓ ) , g k ( ℓ ) ) (F_{k}^{(\ell)},g_{k}^{(\ell)}) , k = 0 , … , N − 1 k=0,\ldots,N-1 , from its own structured coefficients and Brownian increments. Before they are scanned, causal features x k ( ℓ − 1 ) x_{k}^{(\ell-1)} of the previous layer’s path (its normalised state and the time features) produce, through two gated linear units, a diagonal scale α k ( ℓ ) ∈ ( 𝟏 − ε , 𝟏 + ε ) d \alpha_{k}^{(\ell)}\in(\mathbf{1}-\varepsilon,\mathbf{1}+\varepsilon)^{d} and an offset o k ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ d o_{k}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} ; the gate architecture, the construction of the gate input and alternative parameterisations are given in Appendix C.4 . The affine pair is then modified by scaling only the diagonal entries of the transition matrix and by adding the offset correction, F ¯ k ( ℓ ) = 𝒟 ⁡ ( α k ( ℓ ) , F k ( ℓ ) ) and g ¯ k ( ℓ ) = g k ( ℓ ) + o k ( ℓ ) , \bar{F}_{k}^{(\ell)}=\mathcal{D}(\alpha^{(\ell)}_{k},F^{(\ell)}_{k})\qquad\textrm{and }\qquad\bar{g}_{k}^{(\ell)}=g_{k}^{(\ell)}+o_{k}^{(\ell)}, (7) where 𝒟 \mathcal{D} rescales the diagonal of F k ( ℓ ) F^{(\ell)}_{k} entrywise by α k ( ℓ ) \alpha^{(\ell)}_{k} (Appendix C.4 ), and layer ℓ \ell is evaluated by scanning the modified affine recurrence Z k + 1 ( ℓ ) = F ¯ k ( ℓ ) ​ Z k ( ℓ ) + g ¯ k ( ℓ ) . Z_{k+1}^{(\ell)}=\bar{F}_{k}^{(\ell)}Z_{k}^{(\ell)}+\bar{g}_{k}^{(\ell)}. (8) The key point is that gated in-flow introduces nonlinearity through the dependence of ( F ¯ k ( ℓ ) , g ¯ k ( ℓ ) ) (\bar{F}_{k}^{(\ell)},\bar{g}_{k}^{(\ell)}) on the previous path Z ( ℓ − 1 ) Z^{(\ell-1)} , while preserving affine dependence on the current state Z k ( ℓ ) Z_{k}^{(\ell)} ; the recurrence is therefore evaluated exactly by the parallel associative scan (Proposition B.1 (b), Appendix B ).

sections.heading: 3.4 Linear decoder
sections.text: After the final stacking layer, the model maps the last latent path to the observation space through a learned linear readout: Y t = Π o ​ Z t ( L ) , Π o ∈ ℝ p × d , Y_{t}=\Pi_{o}Z_{t}^{(L)},\qquad\Pi_{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d}, (9) where Z ( L ) Z^{(L)} denotes the path produced by the final layer and Π o ∈ Θ \Pi_{o}\in\Theta . When the initial observation is prescribed, we apply an optional shift so that the generated path satisfies the required value at t = 0 t=0 .

sections.heading: 3.5 Discretisation and scan
sections.text: At each time step, every layer builds an affine pair ( F k , g k ) (F_{k},g_{k}) by freezing the time-dependent coefficients of Eq. 6 at t k t_{k} , using either the matrix-exponential or the Euler–Maruyama transition of Appendix C.1 . The previous-layer path then modifies the pairs to ( F ¯ k ( ℓ ) , g ¯ k ( ℓ ) ) (\bar{F}_{k}^{(\ell)},\bar{g}_{k}^{(\ell)}) as in Eq. 7 . Once the previous layers are fixed, each layer is therefore an affine recurrence in its own state, and the modified recurrence is evaluated, layer after layer, by the parallel associative scan of Section 2.1 (Proposition B.1 ); the strong error of the resulting layerwise Euler–Maruyama scheme is of order 1 / 2 1/2 for every fixed depth (Theorem B.1 , Appendix B ).

sections.heading: 4 Last-Layer Girsanov Tilt
sections.text: Calibration losses on rare events receive little signal from plain Monte-Carlo paths under ℙ \mathbb{P} : an event of probability p p estimated from n n paths has relative standard error ( 1 − p ) / ( p ​ n ) \sqrt{(1-p)/(pn)} , so more paths help only as n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} . We therefore simulate under a tilted measure ℚ \mathbb{Q} that visits the rare region more often and reweight by d ​ ℙ / d ​ ℚ \,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}/\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q} ; for diffusion paths Girsanov’s theorem (Appendix A.1 ) gives the ratio in closed form for an adapted drift shift, and choosing the shift as a learned controller yields an importance sampler that acts on the constant 1 / p 1/\sqrt{p} itself. The shift is confined to the final layer, so that the prefix dynamics calibrated by the vanilla loss are not perturbed. The final layer is driven by a partially independent innovation ϵ \epsilon , and only the innovation is tilted: under ℚ \mathbb{Q} it is shifted by an adapted control u θ , k ∈ ℝ m u_{\theta,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} , a function of the innovation history and of stop-gradient features of the prefix latent path, d ​ W k ( L ) \displaystyle\,\mathrm{d}W^{(L)}_{k} = ρ ​ d ​ W k prefix + 1 − ρ 2 ​ d ​ ϵ k , ρ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) , \displaystyle=\rho\,\,\mathrm{d}W^{\mathrm{prefix}}_{k}+\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}\,\,\mathrm{d}\epsilon_{k},\qquad\rho\in[0,1), (10) d ​ ϵ k ℚ \displaystyle\,\mathrm{d}\epsilon^{\mathbb{Q}}_{k} = d ​ ϵ k ℙ − u θ , k ​ d ​ t . \displaystyle=\,\mathrm{d}\epsilon^{\mathbb{P}}_{k}-u_{\theta,k}\,\,\mathrm{d}t. (11) In a gated stack the random initial latent z 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) z_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) carries a large share of the terminal variance, so the tilt also shifts the initial state, z 0 = μ θ + ξ z_{0}=\mu_{\theta}+\xi with ξ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) \xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and a learned μ θ ∈ ℝ d \mu_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . The discrete log-likelihood ratio is then log ⁡ d ​ ℚ d ​ ℙ = μ θ ⊤ ​ z 0 − 1 2 ​ ‖ μ θ ‖ 2 + ∑ k = 0 N − 1 ( u θ , k ⊤ ​ d ​ ϵ k ℙ − 1 2 ​ ‖ u θ , k ‖ 2 ​ d ​ t ) , \log\frac{\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}}{\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}}=\mu_{\theta}^{\top}z_{0}-\tfrac{1}{2}\|\mu_{\theta}\|^{2}+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(u_{\theta,k}^{\top}\,\mathrm{d}\epsilon_{k}^{\mathbb{P}}-\tfrac{1}{2}\|u_{\theta,k}\|^{2}\,\,\mathrm{d}t\right), (12) which is exact, normalised ( 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ d ​ ℙ / d ​ ℚ ] = 1 \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}/\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}]=1 ) and depends only on the control, the shift and the shifted innovation (Theorem 5.2 ). The tilt is a training-time device: the backbone minimises the calibration loss with the far-tail terms estimated on the tilted batch by self-normalised importance sampling, the controller is trained by the cross-entropy method under a wall on KL ( ℚ ∥ ℙ ) \KL(\mathbb{Q}\|\mathbb{P}) , and samples from the trained model are drawn under ℙ \mathbb{P} without it. The rationale for the initial-state shift, the controller, the two objectives and the gradient convention they require are given in Appendix C.5 .

sections.heading: 5 Theoretical Results
sections.text: This section states the guarantees behind the architecture; the assumptions in full, the auxiliary results and all proofs are collected in Appendix B . Three questions are answered here: (i) whether the stacked model is a well-posed stochastic process with moment bounds that do not deteriorate with depth (Theorem 5.1 ); (ii) whether the last-layer change of measure yields exact importance weights (Theorem 5.2 ); (iii) what the class can represent (Theorem 5.3 ). Two further facts are used throughout and are stated and proved in the appendix: (iv) the parallel associative scan returns exactly the sequential iterates of every layer, gated or not, so that the depth- L L stack is evaluated exactly in O ⁡ ( L ​ log ⁡ T ) O(L\log T) parallel depth (Proposition B.1 ); (v) the layerwise Euler–Maruyama scheme, with the gates evaluated on the discrete previous layer, has strong order 1 / 2 1/2 for every fixed depth (Theorem B.1 ).

sections.heading: Standing assumptions.
sections.text: The statements concern the model of Section 3 under three assumptions, stated in full in Appendix B.1 . All of them hold by construction of the architecture; we list them only to fix what the theorems cover. • Model class (Assumption B.1 ): structured affine layers with the time-dependent coefficients of Appendix C.2 , gated in-flow stacking with gates that read the normalised previous-layer state and the time features, arbitrary depth and widths, a linear readout, and a square-integrable initial state whose law may be degenerate. • Coefficients (Assumption B.2 ): the coefficients of every layer are bounded and regular in time. For the ungated base layer this is automatic, because the time features are smooth and the decoders are fixed networks; the gated layers inherit it from the regularity of the previous layer. • Gates (Assumption B.3 ): the gates are causal and Lipschitz in their input path, the flow gate stays within a fixed distance of one, and the offset gate is bounded for every fixed choice of its weights because its input is normalised. The consequence that drives every constant is that the gated coefficients of a layer obey bounds that depend neither on the layer index nor on the depth of the stack. Theorem 5.1 (Well-posedness) . Let q ≥ 2 q\geq 2 and 𝔼 ​ ‖ z 0 ‖ q < ∞ \mathbb{E}\|z_{0}\|^{q}<\infty . (a) Single layer. sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate SLiSDE on three main benchmarks: a path-dependent toy dynamical system ( toy ) and two option-surface datasets ( dax and spx ), where the toy benchmark tests whether a model can match nonlinear long-horizon path statistics generated by a highly nonlinear stochastic dynamical system. Dataset construction, training protocols, and search grids are described in Appendix D . Additional results – ablations over the structural choices, the timing study, distributional recovery on toy and the Girsanov tilt studies – are collected in Appendix E .

sections.heading: Models and baselines.
sections.text: We compare SLiSDE against two baselines: (i) a fully connected Neural SDE with neural drift and diffusion, and (ii) SLiCE ( Walker et al., 2025 ) . SLiCE is a natural structured-sequence baseline because it is a scan-compatible linear CDE and it is more expressive than Mamba ( Gu and Dao, 2023 ) ; in our experiments we drive it with Brownian motion to match the stochastic input used by SLiSDE. For all model families, we report results for both two-layer and three-layer configurations.

For a generic Neural SDE, no analogous parallel associative scan is available, so simulation remains sequential in time. sections.heading: Implementation and Compute.
sections.text: All models and experiments are implemented in JAX. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SLiSDE-3B86/ . All experiments were run on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPU.

sections.heading: 6.1 Path-dependent toy benchmark ( TOY )

The task is to calibrate the model law to the functional targets of Appendix D – thresholded positive parts, running maximum, squared path average and threshold-crossing probabilities at five evaluation times – through the objective of Eq. 5 . In this first experiment, all models are trained without the Girsanov tilt, so the comparison isolates the effect of the architecture and stacking mechanism. Table 2 shows that SLiSDE substantially improves both accuracy and efficiency on the toy path-functional benchmark. The gated in-flow variant achieves the lowest total loss for both L = 2 L=2 and L = 3 L=3 , while using fewer parameters than the Neural SDE and SLiCE baselines. In terms of runtime, SLiSDE remains faster than the Neural SDE baseline, reflecting the benefit of scan-compatible structured dynamics. SLiCE, which shares the parallel associative scan, is not designed for random inputs: it treats the Brownian path as one more input sequence, and its gap shows that deterministic sequence models do not transfer to a task that requires genuinely nonlinear stochastic dynamics. The recovery of the full path law beyond the calibrated targets (Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Wasserstein-1 distances to the ground truth for the terminal value and the running maximum) is reported in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 6.2 Option-surface benchmark ( DAX )
sections.text: dax is a real-data functional calibration benchmark built from historical European option quotes on the DAX index across multiple threshold levels and maturities. The task is to learn a stochastic path generator whose terminal functionals match the observed option surface. For evaluation, we hold out 25 % 25\% of the threshold levels in each target group using a structured non-contiguous mask, so that the model is tested on interpolation across the surface rather than extrapolation outside the observed range. The same protocol is applied to the spx surface (Appendix D ): there SLiSDE matches the held-out loss of SLiCE with two layers and attains the lowest held-out and far-tail loss with three layers, with 6 6 – 8 × 8\times fewer parameters and 3.5 3.5 – 4 × 4\times faster epochs, and both structured models are far ahead of the Neural SDE (Table 4 , Appendix E ). Out-of-the-money (OTM) options correspond to thresholds that are far from the current level of the underlying index, so their value is determined by paths that end in the tails of the distribution. Table 3 shows the real-data benchmark. SLiSDE gated in-flow attains the lowest held-out loss at both depths (with two layers within one standard error of SLiCE) and, with three layers, also the lowest far-tail loss of all models, at a parameter count below SLiCE’s and in about half of its time per epoch; with two layers SLiCE fits the far puts slightly better, within one standard error. sections.heading: Girsanov tilt.
sections.text: With the tilt of Section 4 the far-tail calibration of the dax model improves at a fixed path budget: over seven seeds the mean far-call held-out error falls by about a third relative to the vanilla model ( 0.64 × 0.64\times ; lower on six seeds of seven, paired t t -test on the log-errors p = 0.03 p=0.03 ) and the mean total held-out loss drops by 15 15 – 24 % 24\% , while the budget-matched untilted model is never better on the far tails (Table 9 ). In a controlled rare-event study on toy , the tilt with the vanilla importance-sampling estimator reduces the relative error of plain Monte Carlo at equal budget by a factor of 2 2 to 4 4 , growing with the rarity of the event (Table 10 ); both studies are reported in Appendix E .

sections.heading: Timing.
sections.text: Wall-clock times of full training steps for batch sizes up to 4096 4096 and horizons up to T = 8192 T=8192 are reported in Appendix E . At equal parameter count, SLiSDE evaluated sequentially is 6 6 – 7 × 7\times faster per step than the Neural SDE at B = 64 B=64 and 1.3 1.3 – 1.4 × 1.4\times faster at B = 1024 B=1024 ; only at B = 4096 B=4096 , where the GPU is saturated by batch parallelism, is the Neural SDE step faster ( 179 179 against 242 242 ms).

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced SLiSDE , a family of Neural SDEs that moves nonlinearity from per-step drift and diffusion evaluations to gated in-flow coupling between structured linear stochastic layers. Each layer remains affine in its own state and is therefore parallel-scannable, while cross-layer modulation, time-dependent coefficients, and a learned linear decoder provide expressivity. For tail-sensitive path-functional objectives, we also use a last-layer Girsanov tilt, together with a shift of the initial latent state, with a closed-form Radon–Nikodym correction, yielding a lightweight importance-sampling overlay. We prove well-posedness, scan compatibility, discretisation error bounds, and validity of the change of measure, and that the terminal laws of the gated stack are dense in 𝒫 2 \mathcal{P}_{2} : the structural restrictions cost nothing in expressive power at the level of terminal laws. Empirically, SLiSDE attains a lower calibration loss than the fully neural SDE baseline on every benchmark and at both depths, and trains faster in all but two of the settings tested, the three-layer dax configuration and the largest batch size of the timing study. Against the structured-CDE baseline it is clearly better on toy ; on the option surfaces it attains the lowest mean loss on dax at both depths and on the three-layer spx surface and matches it on the two-layer spx surface, differences that are within one standard error, and with three layers it attains the lowest far-tail error on both surfaces. Throughout, it uses 1.4 1.4 – 8 × 8\times fewer parameters than the structured-CDE baseline and trains 2 2 – 4 × 4\times faster per epoch. The tilt is a variance-reduction device: on toy it reduces the error of rare-event estimates by factors of two to four at equal budget, growing with the rarity of the event, and on the far tails of dax it improves the far-tail calibration of the vanilla model, while budget-matched plain Monte Carlo remains a strong competitor where the targets are not rare. The results suggest that structured linear stochastic layers, combined with selective in-flow coupling and optional importance sampling, are a practical alternative to fully neural drift–diffusion networks for long-horizon functional calibration.

sections.heading: Future work.
sections.text: From the stochastic-analysis point of view, a natural direction is to better understand gated in-flow stacking as a path-dependent transformation of linear diffusions, including its possible connections to filtering. A second direction is to study structured Neural SDEs beyond functional calibration, in particular as continuous-time generative models such as Neural-SDE GANs.

sections.text: Collapse is moreover incompatible with the population objective whenever the target marginal is non-degenerate. If Y t = m t Y_{t}=m_{t} almost surely then 𝔼 ℙ θ ​ [ ( Y t − K ) + ] = ( m t − K ) + , \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\theta}}[(Y_{t}-K)_{+}]=(m_{t}-K)_{+}, a piecewise affine function of K K with a single change of slope at K = m t K=m_{t} , which cannot coincide on an interval with a strictly convex target map K ↦ c t , K K\mapsto c_{t,K} such as an arbitrage-free call surface. We do not claim that a finite collection of such constraints determines the entire path law.

sections.heading: Non-uniqueness and model risk.
sections.text: Finitely many expectation constraints are satisfied by infinitely many diffusions, so ℒ ∞ \mathcal{L}_{\infty} has no unique minimiser. This is a property of functional calibration rather than of the objective: the data are finitely many expectations, so no objective built on them can identify the path law. In derivatives markets one typically has nothing beyond quoted prices, and it is standard practice to work with – and deliberately explore – the multiplicity of models consistent with the same quotes in order to quantify model risk; Gierjatowicz et al. (2020) , for example, use randomised calibrated neural SDEs to obtain price bounds over the calibrated set. Enforcing uniqueness through an auxiliary term would not remove the ambiguity but shift it to the choice of the reference measure. Theorem 5.3 guarantees that the model class itself never restricts what is reachable, so the selection among constraint-consistent processes is driven by the data, the initialisation and the training procedure, never by a hidden limitation of the class. Operationally we validate the selection where a selection can be validated, on functionals the model was never fitted to: the held-out-strike transfer on dax and spx , and the distributional-recovery study on toy (Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Wasserstein-1 distances to the ground-truth simulator, Appendix E ).

sections.heading: Model selection within the calibrated set.
sections.text: There are settings, physics in particular, where prior information is available: a reference dynamics, an equilibrium law, known symmetries. There, an additive penalty turns Eq. 5 into a principled selection rule – a Kullback–Leibler divergence to the available reference ( Smith and others, 2026 ) , a minimal-relative-entropy criterion in the spirit of Avellaneda et al. (1997) for volatility surfaces, or a context-specific penalty – and such terms drop into the training loop unchanged. The framework already computes and uses exactly this quantity where a reference measure genuinely exists: in the Girsanov layer, the controller is trained with a KL ( ℚ ∥ ℙ ) \KL(\mathbb{Q}\|\mathbb{P}) anchor (Appendix C.8 ), the pathwise log Radon–Nikodym exponent that our machinery evaluates, which penalises tilts that move too far from the untilted reference model.

sections.heading: Relation to generative training.
sections.text: Training against a fixed family of statistics can be viewed as a maximum-mean-discrepancy objective with a non-characteristic kernel, a point discussed by Kidger et al. (2021) , who contrast it with their adversarial formulation using a learned discriminator; the variational formulation of Tzen and Raginsky (2019) and the signature-kernel scores of Issa et al. (2023) likewise address a different, generative learning objective that requires sample paths. The method belongs instead to the calibration strand ( Gierjatowicz et al., 2020 ; Cuchiero et al., 2020 ; Cohen et al., 2021 ) , in which prescribed functional expectations, such as derivative prices, are matched.

sections.heading: Appendix B Theoretical Results: Assumptions, Auxiliary Results and Proofs
sections.text: This appendix states the standing assumptions in full, establishes the two auxiliary results used throughout the paper (exactness of the parallel associative scan and the strong discretisation error of the stacked scheme) and proves every result of Section 5 . It is organised as follows. • Appendix B.1 states the assumptions and proves Lemma 1 : a gated layer inherits the coefficient bounds of its base layer with constants that do not depend on the depth. Every later constant rests on this lemma. • Appendix B.2 proves Theorem 5.1 , first for one layer with random coefficients (Lemma 2 ) and then by induction over the layers. • Appendix B.3 proves Proposition B.1 , the exactness of the scan. • Appendix B.4 proves Theorem B.1 in four steps: one-step moments (Lemma 3 ), discrete stability (Lemma 4 ), the Euler–Maruyama error of one layer (Lemma 5 ) and an induction over the layers that carries a doubled moment order at every step down the stack. • Appendices B.5 and B.6 prove Theorems 5.2 and 5.3 .

sections.heading: Appendix C Implementation Details
sections.text: This appendix expands the implementation choices summarised in the main text. All reported SLiSDE results use the gated in-flow stack (Section 3.3 ) with structured block-diagonal base layers, an always-on RMS normalisation of the gate input, optional causal convolutions, and time-feature augmentation; residual stacking is not used. The Girsanov tilt described in Section 4 is applied only to the final layer, with the correlated-driver construction of Eq. 10 .

sections.heading: C.1 Discretisation of a linear layer
sections.text: On the interval [ t k , t k + 1 ] [t_{k},t_{k+1}] , the affine linear SDE Eq. 2 admits the exponential approximation Z k + 1 = F k Z k + g k , g k = b Δ t + D Δ W k , F k = exp ⁡ ( ( A − 1 2 ​ ∑ j = 1 m ( C j ) 2 ) ​ Δ ​ t + ∑ j = 1 m C j ​ Δ ​ W k j ) . \begin{gathered}Z_{k+1}=F_{k}Z_{k}+g_{k},\qquad g_{k}=b\Delta t+D\Delta W_{k},\\ F_{k}=\exp\left(\left(A-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{m}(C^{j})^{2}\right)\Delta t+\sum_{j=1}^{m}C^{j}\,\Delta W_{k}^{j}\right).\end{gathered} (77) The correction is the Itô correction. If A , C 1 , … , C m A,C^{1},\ldots,C^{m} commute pairwise, then F k F_{k} is the exact flow of the homogeneous Itô equation; otherwise it is an exponential approximation. The affine term g k g_{k} remains a first-order approximation. To avoid computing matrix exponentials, we use the Euler–Maruyama transition Z k + 1 = ( I + A ​ Δ ​ t + ∑ j = 1 m C j ​ Δ ​ W k j ) ​ Z k + b ​ Δ ​ t + D ​ Δ ​ W k , Z_{k+1}=\left(I+A\Delta t+\sum_{j=1}^{m}C^{j}\,\Delta W_{k}^{j}\right)Z_{k}+b\Delta t+D\Delta W_{k}, (78) which preserves the affine recurrence structure and is used throughout our experiments. With the time-dependent coefficients of Appendix C.2 , the static coefficients are replaced by their values at t k t_{k} in both transitions; the strong error of the Euler–Maruyama scheme is analysed in Appendix B.4 .

sections.heading: C.2 Time-dependent coefficient map
sections.text: Each base layer (Section 3.1 ) stores static structured coefficients ( A , b , C 1 , … , C m , d 1 , … , d m ) (A,b,C^{1},\ldots,C^{m},d^{1},\ldots,d^{m}) and can be made time-dependent through a small deterministic decoder. For each grid time t k t_{k} we form τ ⁡ ( t k ) = ( 1 , t k , t k 2 , sin ⁡ ( ω ​ t k ) , cos ⁡ ( ω ​ t k ) ) , h ⁡ ( t k ) = tanh ⁡ ( U ​ τ ​ ( t k ) + c ) , \tau(t_{k})=\bigl(1,\,t_{k},\,t_{k}^{2},\,\sin(\omega t_{k}),\,\cos(\omega t_{k})\bigr),\qquad h(t_{k})=\tanh\bigl(U\tau(t_{k})+c\bigr), and add structure-aware corrections to the free coefficient entries: A t k = A + Δ ​ A ​ ( h ⁡ ( t k ) ) , b t k = b + Δ ​ b ​ ( h ⁡ ( t k ) ) , C t k j = C j + Δ ​ C j ​ ( h ⁡ ( t k ) ) . A_{t_{k}}=A+\Delta A\bigl(h(t_{k})\bigr),\quad b_{t_{k}}=b+\Delta b\bigl(h(t_{k})\bigr),\quad C_{t_{k}}^{j}=C^{j}+\Delta C^{j}\bigl(h(t_{k})\bigr). For additive diffusion we use a per-Brownian-channel time gate on the dense diffusion matrix, equivalently producing d t k j d_{t_{k}}^{j} from d j d^{j} and h ⁡ ( t k ) h(t_{k}) . The decoders respect the chosen matrix structure: diagonal layers decode only diagonal entries, block-diagonal layers decode only block entries, and dense layers decode full matrices. Decoders are zero-initialised, so the model starts from the time-homogeneous structured SDE and learns time variation only when useful.

sections.heading: C.3 Feature conditioning in gated layers
sections.text: The gated layer consumes the previous layer path at the same time grid as the current layer. The simplest gate input is Norm ⁡ ( Z k ( ℓ − 1 ) ) \operatorname{Norm}(Z_{k}^{(\ell-1)}) , where Z k ( ℓ − 1 ) Z_{k}^{(\ell-1)} is the model output after ℓ − 1 \ell-1 layers and the normalisation is RMSNorm or LayerNorm (RMSNorm by default, applied at every gated layer). Note that normalisation controls the scale of the gate input but does not by itself bound the paths; the offset gate is nevertheless bounded for every fixed choice of its weights, which is what the analysis uses (Appendix B.1 ). In the implementation this signal can be enriched in two ways.

sections.heading: Causal convolution (for gated-in-flow stacking only).
sections.text: Before normalisation, the previous-layer path can be passed through a left-padded depthwise causal convolution along the time axis. The value at time t k t_{k} depends only on previous-layer states up to t k t_{k} , so the gate is adapted and does not leak future information. The convolution is wrapped in a residual update and its kernel is small at initialisation, making the initial behaviour close to the no-convolution case while still allowing the gate to learn short temporal summaries.

sections.heading: Time features.
sections.text: The deterministic vector τ gate ​ ( t ) = ( t , t 2 , sin ⁡ ( ω ​ t ) , cos ⁡ ( ω ​ t ) ) \tau_{\mathrm{gate}}(t)=(t,t^{2},\sin(\omega t),\cos(\omega t)) (79) can be concatenated to the gate input after convolution and after normalisation. Appending time features after normalisation preserves their scale, while keeping the convolution focused on the stochastic path rather than on deterministic batch-constant signals. With both refinements, the gate input is x k = [ Norm ⁡ ( CausalConv ⁡ ( H ( ℓ − 1 ) ) k ) , t k , t k 2 , sin ⁡ ( ω ​ t k ) , cos ⁡ ( ω ​ t k ) ] . x_{k}=\bigl[\operatorname{Norm}\left(\operatorname{CausalConv}(H^{(\ell-1)})_{k}\right),t_{k},t_{k}^{2},\sin(\omega t_{k}),\cos(\omega t_{k})\bigr]. (80)

sections.heading: C.4 Gated in-flow implementation
sections.text: The paper focuses on the gated in-flow stacking. Given the conditioned feature x k ( ℓ − 1 ) x_{k}^{(\ell-1)} from Eq. 80 , the layer constructs a bounded diagonal scale α k ( ℓ ) = 𝟏 + ε ​ σ ​ ( W g ​ F ( ℓ ) ​ x k ( ℓ − 1 ) ) ⊙ tanh ⁡ ( W i ​ F ( ℓ ) ​ x k ( ℓ − 1 ) ) , \alpha_{k}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{1}+\varepsilon\,\sigma\bigl(W_{gF}^{(\ell)}x_{k}^{(\ell-1)}\bigr)\odot\tanh\bigl(W_{iF}^{(\ell)}x_{k}^{(\ell-1)}\bigr), (81) and an affine residual offset o k ( ℓ ) = σ ⁡ ( W g ​ o ( ℓ ) ​ x k ( ℓ − 1 ) ) ⊙ ( W i ​ o ( ℓ ) ​ x k ( ℓ − 1 ) + c i ​ o ( ℓ ) ) . o_{k}^{(\ell)}=\sigma\bigl(W_{go}^{(\ell)}x_{k}^{(\ell-1)}\bigr)\odot\bigl(W_{io}^{(\ell)}x_{k}^{(\ell-1)}+c_{io}^{(\ell)}\bigr). (82) All gate maps carry trainable biases, omitted from the displays except c i ​ o ( ℓ ) c_{io}^{(\ell)} . The tanh \tanh bound gives α k ( ℓ ) ∈ ( 𝟏 − ε , 𝟏 + ε ) \alpha_{k}^{(\ell)}\in(\mathbf{1}-\varepsilon,\mathbf{1}+\varepsilon) coordinatewise. The scale α k ( ℓ ) \alpha_{k}^{(\ell)} is applied only to the diagonal entries of the structured drift matrix F k ( ℓ ) F_{k}^{(\ell)} , and the offset o k ( ℓ ) o_{k}^{(\ell)} is added to the affine intercept g k ( ℓ ) g_{k}^{(\ell)} . The offset o k ( ℓ ) o_{k}^{(\ell)} is an unbounded GLU: the gate σ ⁡ ( W g ​ o ( ℓ ) ​ x k ( ℓ − 1 ) ) \sigma(W_{go}^{(\ell)}x_{k}^{(\ell-1)}) is bounded, while the value branch W i ​ o ( ℓ ) ​ x k ( ℓ − 1 ) + c i ​ o ( ℓ ) W_{io}^{(\ell)}x_{k}^{(\ell-1)}+c_{io}^{(\ell)} is linear in the gate input. Because the gate input is normalised and therefore lies in a ball of radius Λ x \Lambda_{x} , ‖ o k ( ℓ ) ‖ ≤ ‖ W i ​ o ( ℓ ) ‖ ​ Λ x + ‖ c i ​ o ( ℓ ) ‖ \|o_{k}^{(\ell)}\|\leq\|W^{(\ell)}_{io}\|\Lambda_{x}+\|c^{(\ell)}_{io}\| for every fixed choice of weights, which is the boundedness used in Appendix B ; the magnitude itself is free, which is what the proof of Theorem 5.3 exploits. The drift scale α k ( ℓ ) \alpha_{k}^{(\ell)} is applied only to the diagonal entries of the structured transition matrix F k ( ℓ ) F_{k}^{(\ell)} (a diagonal, row-wise Hadamard action), while o k ( ℓ ) o_{k}^{(\ell)} is added directly to the affine intercept g k ( ℓ ) g_{k}^{(\ell)} with no additional Δ ​ t \Delta t factor. sections.heading: C.5 Last-layer Girsanov tilt: design details
sections.text: This subsection collects the design choices behind Section 4 .

sections.heading: Why the initial state is tilted.
sections.text: The innovation of the final layer is not the only source of randomness the rare event depends on. In a gated stack the random initial latent z 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) z_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) carries a large share of the terminal variance – on the toy model of Section 6 the final-layer innovation explains only about a quarter of Var ⁡ ( Y T ) \operatorname{Var}(Y_{T}) – and a controller acting on the innovation alone cannot reach the rare region: every such variant we trained kept the hit rate of the tilted paths at the plain Monte-Carlo level for p ≤ 10 − 3 p\leq 10^{-3} . Under ℚ \mathbb{Q} , z 0 = μ θ + ξ z_{0}=\mu_{\theta}+\xi with ξ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) \xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and a learned μ θ ∈ ℝ d \mu_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (one per controller), which contributes the closed-form factor μ θ ⊤ ​ z 0 − 1 2 ​ ‖ μ θ ‖ 2 \mu_{\theta}^{\top}z_{0}-\tfrac{1}{2}\|\mu_{\theta}\|^{2} of Eq. 12 to the log-likelihood ratio and 1 2 ​ ‖ μ θ ‖ 2 \tfrac{1}{2}\|\mu_{\theta}\|^{2} to KL ( ℚ ∥ ℙ ) \KL(\mathbb{Q}\|\mathbb{P}) . The prefix driver W prefix W^{\mathrm{prefix}} keeps its law, so the prefix layers are computed by the same map under both measures; only the distribution of their starting point moves.

sections.heading: Controller.
sections.text: The control u θ , k u_{\theta,k} is an adapted function of the reference innovation history { d ​ ϵ j ℙ } j < k \{\,\mathrm{d}\epsilon_{j}^{\mathbb{P}}\}_{j<k} and of stop-gradient features of the prefix latent path { L j ( L − 1 ) } j ≤ k \{L_{j}^{(L-1)}\}_{j\leq k} ; it is parameterised by the diagonal state-space recurrence of Appendix C.6 , driven by both inputs, with recurrence rates constrained to ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) and zero drift at initialisation.

sections.heading: Objectives and gradient convention.
sections.text: Backbone and controller are trained on different objectives with separate optimisers. The backbone minimises the calibration loss, in which each far-tail term is estimated on the tilted batch by self-normalised importance sampling (Appendix C.7 ), combined with the plain estimate on the reference batch in proportion to the two effective sample sizes. The controller is trained by the cross-entropy method: it minimises a Monte-Carlo estimate of KL ( ℚ ⋆ ∥ ℚ θ ) \KL(\mathbb{Q}^{\star}\|\mathbb{Q}_{\theta}) , where ℚ ⋆ ∝ | G | ​ ℙ \mathbb{Q}^{\star}\propto|G|\,\mathbb{P} is the zero-variance proposal of the rare-event functional, under a quadratic wall on KL ( ℚ θ ∥ ℙ ) \KL(\mathbb{Q}_{\theta}\|\mathbb{P}) that keeps the proposal in the regime where the weights remain usable (Appendix C.8 ). The gradient convention matters: the cross-entropy objective is a score-function estimator and requires the log-ratio Eq. 12 to be differentiated with the sampled path held fixed, whereas Monte-Carlo functionals of the weights, such as the KL wall, require the reparameterised form in which the tilted noise is held fixed; the two forms have the same value and different fixed points, and using the reparameterised one for the cross-entropy objective drives the tilt away without bound.

sections.heading: Which estimator.
sections.text: Because the ratio is normalised, the vanilla importance-sampling estimator n q − 1 ​ ∑ i w i ​ G ​ ( X ( i ) ) n_{q}^{-1}\sum_{i}w_{i}G(X^{(i)}) is unbiased. For the calibration loss we use the self-normalised estimator (Appendix C.7 ): the weights are computed pathwise in log-space, self-normalisation is invariant to a common log-shift, so a max-shift can be applied before exponentiation and no single extreme path can dominate through overflow, the ratio form cancels weight fluctuations shared by numerator and denominator, and its O ⁡ ( 1 / n q ) O(1/n_{q}) bias is negligible at our operating point. For rare-event probabilities the vanilla estimator is the better one: the initial-state shift gives large weights to tilted paths that do not reach the event, and those paths enter only the normalisation of the self-normalised estimator. Both estimators are compared in Appendix E .

sections.heading: C.6 Girsanov controller
sections.text: The controller returns an adapted sequence u θ , k ∈ ℝ m u_{\theta,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} that enters the Radon–Nikodym formula Eq. 12 . It is a diagonal state-space recurrence with two branches, one driven by the tilted innovation and one by the stop-gradient prefix latent path, s k + 1 W = diag ( r W ) s k W + U W Δ ϵ ℚ k , s k + 1 Z = diag ( r Z ) s k Z + U Z L k ( L − 1 ) , u θ , k = W mix ​ [ s k W , s k Z ] + c , \begin{gathered}s_{k+1}^{W}=\operatorname{diag}(r_{W})\,s_{k}^{W}+U_{W}\,\Delta\epsilon^{\mathbb{Q}}_{k},\qquad s_{k+1}^{Z}=\operatorname{diag}(r_{Z})\,s_{k}^{Z}+U_{Z}\,L_{k}^{(L-1)},\\ u_{\theta,k}=W_{\mathrm{mix}}\bigl[s_{k}^{W},s_{k}^{Z}\bigr]+c,\end{gathered} so that u θ , k u_{\theta,k} depends on the increments before step k k only. The recurrence is itself affine and can be scanned in parallel.

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: Three details proved necessary. (i) The recurrence rates of both branches are parameterised as exp ⁡ ( − softplus ⁡ ( − r ) ) ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \exp(-\operatorname{softplus}(-r))\in(0,1) , initialised at 0.9997 0.9997 , because an unconstrained rate can drift above one, after which the recurrence grows geometrically over the horizon and overflows, producing non-finite weights. (ii) The mixing weights of the latent-path branch are initialised at zero, so that the untrained controller is the identity tilt with KL ( ℚ ∥ ℙ ) = 0 \KL(\mathbb{Q}\|\mathbb{P})=0 ; with a small random initialisation the branch, which integrates the O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) prefix latent over the whole horizon, gives the untrained controller a divergence of about 8 8 nats per controller, i.e. a collapsed proposal before any training. (iii) The initial-state shift μ θ \mu_{\theta} is a free vector per controller initialised at zero. Controller parameters are trained by Adam with learning rate 2 ⋅ 10 − 3 2\cdot 10^{-3} and gradient clipping at norm one, separately from the backbone optimiser: with a single optimiser and a shared global-norm clip, the cross-entropy gradient, three orders of magnitude larger than the calibration gradient, scaled the backbone updates to zero after the controller was activated.

sections.heading: C.7 Self-normalised importance sampling and ESS
sections.text: Given tilted samples { X ( i ) } i = 1 n q \{X^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n_{q}} drawn under ℚ \mathbb{Q} with unnormalised weights w i = d ​ ℙ d ​ ℚ ​ ( X ( i ) ) , w_{i}=\frac{\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}}{\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}}(X^{(i)}), the self-normalised importance-sampling (SNIS) estimator of 𝔼 ℙ ​ [ G ] \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[G] is 𝔼 ^ ℙ , SNIS ​ [ G ] = ∑ i = 1 n q w i ​ G ​ ( X ( i ) ) ∑ i = 1 n q w i . \widehat{\mathbb{E}}^{\mathbb{P},\mathrm{SNIS}}[G]=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}w_{i}G(X^{(i)})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}w_{i}}. (83) The estimator is biased at finite n q n_{q} but consistent. We monitor the quality of the tilted sample through the effective sample size ESS = ( ∑ i = 1 n q w i ) 2 ∑ i = 1 n q w i 2 ∈ [ 1 , n q ] . \ESS=\frac{\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}w_{i}\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}w_{i}^{2}}\in[1,n_{q}]. (84) ESS = n q \ESS=n_{q} iff all weights are equal; ESS = 1 \ESS=1 iff one weight dominates. In practice we compute the log-weights log ⁡ w i = log ⁡ ( d ​ ℙ / d ​ ℚ ) ​ ( X ( i ) ) \log w_{i}=\log(\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}/\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q})(X^{(i)}) directly from the discrete Radon–Nikodym density Eq. 12 and normalise them with a numerically stable log-sum-exp, so that the SNIS estimator Eq. 83 and the ESS \ESS ratio remain well behaved even when a few tilted paths dominate. In training logs we report the ratio ESS / n q ∈ [ 1 / n q , 1 ] \ESS/n_{q}\in[1/n_{q},1] for comparability across batch sizes; a controller that drives ESS / n q \ESS/n_{q} toward 1 / n q 1/n_{q} signals weight collapse and is held back by the KL wall of Appendix C.8 . For rare-event probabilities we report the vanilla estimator n q − 1 ​ ∑ i w i ​ G ​ ( X ( i ) ) n_{q}^{-1}\sum_{i}w_{i}G(X^{(i)}) as the primary one: with the initial-state shift, tilted paths that do not reach the event can carry large weights, which affect only the denominator of Eq. 83 and make the self-normalised estimator markedly worse (Table 11 ). Its truncated variant caps the weights at n q ​ 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ w ] = n q \sqrt{n_{q}}\,\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[w]=\sqrt{n_{q}} , using the known mean rather than the sample mean, which the very weights to be tamed would inflate.

sections.heading: Backbone.
sections.text: The backbone parameters minimise the calibration loss Eq. 5 . Terms that involve a rare-event functional G G are estimated on the tilted batch by the self-normalised estimator Eq. 83 , and, in the combined variant, averaged with the plain estimate on the reference batch of size n p n_{p} with the weights n p / ( n p + ESS ) n_{p}/(n_{p}+\ESS) and ESS / ( n p + ESS ) \ESS/(n_{p}+\ESS) , held fixed for the gradient; all other terms are plain Monte-Carlo estimates on the reference batch. The backbone receives no gradient through the weights.

sections.heading: Controller.
sections.text: The controller parameters θ c = ( u θ , μ θ ) \theta_{c}=(u_{\theta},\mu_{\theta}) minimise the cross-entropy objective with a KL wall, 𝒥 ^ ( θ c ) = − ∑ i = 1 n q w ¯ ⋆ i log d ​ ℚ θ c d ​ ℙ ( X ( i ) ) + λ KL KL ^ ( ℚ θ c ∥ ℙ ) + ( KL ^ ( ℚ θ c ∥ ℙ ) − κ ) + 2 , w ¯ i ⋆ ∝ | G ⁡ ( X ( i ) ) | ​ d ​ ℙ d ​ ℚ θ c ​ ( X ( i ) ) , \begin{gathered}\widehat{\mathcal{J}}(\theta_{c})=-\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}\bar{w}^{\star}_{i}\,\log\frac{\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}_{\theta_{c}}}{\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}}(X^{(i)})+\lambda_{\KL}\,\widehat{\KL}(\mathbb{Q}_{\theta_{c}}\|\mathbb{P})+\bigl(\widehat{\KL}(\mathbb{Q}_{\theta_{c}}\|\mathbb{P})-\kappa\bigr)_{+}^{2},\\ \bar{w}^{\star}_{i}\propto|G(X^{(i)})|\,\frac{\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}}{\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}_{\theta_{c}}}(X^{(i)}),\end{gathered} (85) where the self-normalised target weights w ¯ i ⋆ \bar{w}^{\star}_{i} are held fixed for the gradient (their log-ratios clipped at ± 5 \pm 5 so that no single path can dominate the update), κ \kappa is the wall in nats ( 6 6 on dax ; − log ⁡ p + 2 -\log p+2 for an event of nominal probability p p on toy ), and KL ^ \widehat{\KL} is the energy form n q − 1 ​ ∑ i ( 1 2 ​ ∑ k ‖ u θ , k ‖ 2 ​ Δ ​ t + 1 2 ​ ‖ μ θ ‖ 2 ) n_{q}^{-1}\sum_{i}\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{k}\|u_{\theta,k}\|^{2}\Delta t+\tfrac{1}{2}\|\mu_{\theta}\|^{2}\bigr) , whose ℚ \mathbb{Q} -expectation equals KL ( ℚ ∥ ℙ ) \KL(\mathbb{Q}\|\mathbb{P}) exactly. The first term is the Monte-Carlo estimate of KL ( ℚ ⋆ ∥ ℚ θ c ) \KL(\mathbb{Q}^{\star}\|\mathbb{Q}_{\theta_{c}}) up to a constant, with ℚ ⋆ ∝ | G | ​ ℙ \mathbb{Q}^{\star}\propto|G|\,\mathbb{P} the zero-variance proposal; its minimiser is the moment match 𝔼 ℚ ⋆ \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\star}} of the sufficient statistics of the tilt (the conditional mean of z 0 z_{0} and of the innovation increments given the rare event). The wall is needed because the weak penalty λ KL = 10 − 4 \lambda_{\KL}=10^{-4} alone does not prevent the collapse of the proposal onto a handful of paths once the target weights degenerate.

sections.heading: Gradient convention.
sections.text: Eq. 12 can be differentiated in two ways with the same value. In the score form the sampled path is held fixed: ∂ u θ , k log ⁡ ( d ​ ℚ / d ​ ℙ ) = Δ ​ ϵ k ℚ \partial_{u_{\theta,k}}\log(\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}/\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P})=\Delta\epsilon^{\mathbb{Q}}_{k} and ∂ μ θ = z 0 − μ θ \partial_{\mu_{\theta}}=z_{0}-\mu_{\theta} , the scores of the tilted law, which is what the cross-entropy term requires. In the reparameterised form the tilted noise is held fixed and the derivative is Δ ​ ϵ k ℙ \Delta\epsilon^{\mathbb{P}}_{k} (respectively z 0 z_{0} ), which is the correct total derivative of a ℚ \mathbb{Q} -expectation of a function of the weights, such as the KL wall or the effective sample size. Using the reparameterised form inside the cross-entropy term gives an update whose fixed point is not the moment match and which pushes the tilt outward without bound.

sections.heading: toy Dataset
sections.text: toy is a controlled synthetic benchmark designed to separate path fitting from path-functional calibration. The ground truth is a three-component nonlinear Itô SDE on [ 0 , T ] [0,T] with T = 1 T=1 , state X t = ( X t 1 , X t 2 , X t 3 ) X_{t}=(X^{1}_{t},X^{2}_{t},X^{3}_{t}) and diagonal state-dependent diffusion: d ​ X t 1 \displaystyle\,\mathrm{d}X^{1}_{t} = − X t 1 ​ ( ( X t 1 ) 2 − 1 ) ​ d ​ t + | X t 1 | + 1 ​ X t 1 + 5 3 ​ d ​ W t 1 , \displaystyle=-X^{1}_{t}\bigl((X^{1}_{t})^{2}-1\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{|X^{1}_{t}|+1}\sqrt[3]{X^{1}_{t}+5}\,\mathrm{d}W^{1}_{t}, X 0 1 \displaystyle X^{1}_{0} = 0.5 , \displaystyle=0.5, d ​ X t 2 \displaystyle\,\mathrm{d}X^{2}_{t} = sin ⁡ ( X t 2 ) ​ ( 2 − ( X t 2 ) 2 ) ​ d ​ t + 1 + ( X t 2 ) 2 3 ​ d ​ W t 2 , \displaystyle=\sin(X^{2}_{t})\bigl(2-(X^{2}_{t})^{2}\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt[3]{1+(X^{2}_{t})^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}W^{2}_{t}, X 0 2 \displaystyle X^{2}_{0} = 0 , \displaystyle=0, d ​ X t 3 \displaystyle\,\mathrm{d}X^{3}_{t} = ( X t 3 − ( X t 3 ) 3 / 3 ) d t + exp ( − ( X t 3 ) 2 / 4 ) X t 3 d W t 3 , \displaystyle=\bigl(X^{3}_{t}-(X^{3}_{t})^{3}/3\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t+\exp\bigl(-(X^{3}_{t})^{2}/4\bigr)\,X^{3}_{t}\,\,\mathrm{d}W^{3}_{t}, X 0 3 \displaystyle X^{3}_{0} = 1 , \displaystyle=1, with mutually independent driving Brownians. The observable is the linear combination Y t = 0.40 ​ X t 1 + 0.35 ​ X t 2 + 0.25 ​ X t 3 . Y_{t}=0.40\,X^{1}_{t}+0.35\,X^{2}_{t}+0.25\,X^{3}_{t}. We simulate 2 × 10 5 2{\times}10^{5} Monte-Carlo paths via Euler–Maruyama on a uniform grid of N = 2048 N=2048 steps. From the simulated paths we compute four classes of supervised path-functional targets at the evaluation times T i ∈ 𝒯 = { 0.1 , 0.25 , 0.5 , 0.75 , 1.0 } T_{i}\in\mathcal{T}=\{0.1,\,0.25,\,0.5,\,0.75,\,1.0\} . These targets are: • Thresholded positive-part functionals at levels 𝒦 = { − 0.5 , − 0.25 , 0 , 0.25 , 0.5 , 0.75 , 1.0 } \mathcal{K}=\{-0.5,-0.25,0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\} : 𝔼 ⁡ [ max ⁡ ( Y T i − K , 0 ) ] . \mathbb{E}[\max(Y_{T_{i}}-K,0)]. • Running maximum : 𝔼 ⁡ [ max 0 ≤ t ≤ T i ⁡ Y t ] . \mathbb{E}[\max_{0\leq t\leq T_{i}}Y_{t}]. • Squared path average : 𝔼 ⁡ [ 1 T i ​ ∫ 0 T i Y t 2 ​ 𝑑 t ] , \mathbb{E}\bigl[\tfrac{1}{T_{i}}\int_{0}^{T_{i}}Y_{t}^{2}\,\,\mathrm{d}t\bigr], computed on the discrete grid. • Threshold-crossing probabilities ℙ ⁡ ( max 0 ≤ t ≤ T i ⁡ Y t ≥ H j ) \mathbb{P}(\max_{0\leq t\leq T_{i}}Y_{t}\geq H_{j}) at three threshold levels H j H_{j} chosen as the 80 % 80\% , 90 % 90\% , and 95 % 95\% empirical quantiles of the terminal running maximum; in the objective the indicator is replaced by a smooth approximation (a sigmoid of the excess over the threshold with a fixed temperature), so that Eq. 5 is differentiable. The threshold-crossing and high-level positive-part targets are deliberately tail-sensitive path functionals. Errors on typical-path statistics and on tail functionals need not agree: a model may fit typical trajectories well while still missing the rare excursions or extrema that determine these calibration targets. Thus toy provides a controlled setting for evaluating whether a model can match both ordinary path behaviour and rare path-dependent statistics.

sections.heading: DAX Dataset
sections.text: dax is a real-data functional calibration benchmark built from historical European option quotes on the DAX index. The purpose of the benchmark is to test whether a stochastic path generator can match a large collection of expectations of nonlinear functions of its terminal value. Each option quote is treated as a supervised target of the form 𝔼 ⁡ [ φ ⁡ ( Y T , K ) ] , \mathbb{E}[\varphi(Y_{T};K)], where Y Y is the generated one-dimensional path, T T is the evaluation time, K K is a threshold level, and φ \varphi is a payoff function. All thresholds and target values are normalised by the spot level S 0 = 25,280 S_{0}=25{,}280 , so that the generated process starts from Y 0 = 1 Y_{0}=1 and K norm = K / S 0 K_{\mathrm{norm}}=K/S_{0} .

sections.heading: Option payoffs (for the non-specialist).
sections.text: A European option on the index with maturity T T and strike K K pays a fixed function of the terminal value Y T Y_{T} alone. The two basic instruments are the call and the put , with payoffs φ call ​ ( Y T , K ) = ( Y T − K ) + , φ put ​ ( Y T , K ) = ( K − Y T ) + , ( x ) + := max ⁡ ( x , 0 ) . \varphi_{\mathrm{call}}(Y_{T};K)=(Y_{T}-K)_{+},\qquad\varphi_{\mathrm{put}}(Y_{T};K)=(K-Y_{T})_{+},\qquad(x)_{+}:=\max(x,0). (86) Under the normalised, discounting-free pricing convention used here, the quoted price of an option is the expectation c T , K = 𝔼 ⁡ [ φ ⁡ ( Y T , K ) ] , c_{T,K}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\varphi(Y_{T};K)\bigr], (87) which is exactly the supervised target above. A strike is at-the-money when K ≈ S 0 K\approx S_{0} (i.e. K norm ≈ 1 K_{\mathrm{norm}}\approx 1 ), in-the-money when the option would pay out if exercised at the current level, and out-of-the-money (OTM) otherwise, that is, a call with K > S 0 K>S_{0} or a put with K < S 0 K<S_{0} . OTM prices are small and depend only on the tails of the terminal law, which is why the far-tail groups are the hardest part of the benchmark. The threshold-indicator targets approximate digital payoffs through finite differences of nearby put prices in the strike, ℙ ⁡ ( Y T ≤ K ) = ∂ K 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( K − Y T ) + ] ≈ 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( K + h − Y T ) + ] − 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( K − h − Y T ) + ] 2 ​ h , \mathbb{P}(Y_{T}\leq K)=\partial_{K}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[(K-Y_{T})_{+}\bigr]\approx\frac{\mathbb{E}\bigl[(K+h-Y_{T})_{+}\bigr]-\mathbb{E}\bigl[(K-h-Y_{T})_{+}\bigr]}{2h}, (88) and analogously ℙ ( Y T > K ) = − ∂ K 𝔼 [ ( Y T − K ) + ] \mathbb{P}(Y_{T}>K)=-\partial_{K}\,\mathbb{E}[(Y_{T}-K)_{+}] from call prices. The dataset is intentionally dense: at each available maturity we include several groups of terminal functionals covering both typical and tail regions of the path distribution: • 25 25 positive-part upper-tail targets, K norm ∈ [ 0.88 , 1.12 ] K_{\mathrm{norm}}\in[0.88,1.12] , corresponding to 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( Y T − K ) + ] \mathbb{E}[(Y_{T}-K)_{+}] ; • 25 25 positive-part lower-tail targets, K norm ∈ [ 0.88 , 1.12 ] K_{\mathrm{norm}}\in[0.88,1.12] , corresponding to 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( K − Y T ) + ] \mathbb{E}[(K-Y_{T})_{+}] ; • 20 20 far lower-tail targets, K norm ∈ [ 0.60 , 0.88 ] K_{\mathrm{norm}}\in[0.60,0.88] ; • 15 15 far upper-tail targets, K norm ∈ [ 1.08 , 1.35 ] K_{\mathrm{norm}}\in[1.08,1.35] ; • 12 12 threshold-indicator targets, synthesised from differences of nearby lower-tail positive-part targets, K norm ∈ [ 0.65 , 0.98 ] K_{\mathrm{norm}}\in[0.65,0.98] . The target threshold levels are evenly spaced on each interval and are matched to the nearest observed threshold in the raw quote table. Maturity indices are recomputed on the model time grid with T = 1 T=1 and N = 1024 N=1024 steps. The far-tail groups are the most challenging part of the benchmark because they depend on rare terminal events under the generated path distribution. When the Girsanov overlay is used for dax , we use two separate controllers : one targets the far lower-tail functionals and the other targets the far upper-tail functionals. This lets each controller focus on a different rare region of path space, rather than requiring a single tilt to cover both tails simultaneously. Train/eval split. Evaluation uses a structured hold-out over strike levels. For each group of targets, one quarter of the strikes are held out for evaluation and the remaining entries are used for training. The held-out strikes are selected non-contiguously, so that the training and evaluation sets cover overlapping ranges. This tests interpolation across the surface rather than extrapolation outside the observed range.

sections.heading: SPX Dataset
sections.text: spx is a second real-data option-surface benchmark, constructed identically to dax but from historical European option quotes on the S&P 500 index. As for dax , each quote is a supervised target 𝔼 ⁡ [ φ ⁡ ( Y T , K ) ] \mathbb{E}[\varphi(Y_{T};K)] with the call and put payoffs defined above; all strikes and target values are normalised by the spot level so that Y 0 = 1 Y_{0}=1 and K norm = K / S 0 K_{\mathrm{norm}}=K/S_{0} , and maturities are recomputed on the model grid with T = 1 T=1 and N = 1024 N=1024 steps. The surface is organised into the same five target groups (near-tail calls and puts, far lower- and upper-tail targets, and threshold-indicator targets) spanning comparable normalised-strike ranges, and evaluation uses the same structured non-contiguous 25 % 25\% strike hold-out, testing interpolation across the surface. When the Girsanov overlay is used, we again employ two controllers, one per far tail. spx serves as an out-of-sample check that the architecture and calibration procedure transfer across underlyings; results are reported in Table 4 of Appendix E .

sections.heading: Training protocol
sections.text: All models use the same optimiser and learning-rate schedule unless otherwise stated: AdamW with β = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) \beta=(0.9,0.999) , peak learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , 100 100 warm-up steps followed by cosine decay, gradient clipping at 1 1 , batch size 1024 1024 , evaluation batch size 2048 2048 , 1 000 1\,000 epochs and seven seeds per configuration; every reported number is a mean ± \pm standard error over the seven seeds of the cell in question. The models are simulated on N = 512 N=512 time steps. SLiSDE uses the offset gate of Eq. 82 with the RMS-normalised gate input; the search grids are listed in Appendix D , and the best cell per family and depth is reported. For Girsanov runs the controller is kept inactive for the first 200 200 epochs. After activation each training step simulates 1 024 1\,024 reference paths and two tilted batches of 512 512 paths, one per controller (far puts, far calls), with ρ = 0 \rho=0 . Each far-tail term is estimated by self-normalised importance sampling on its tilted batch, combined with the plain estimate on the reference batch in proportion to the effective sample sizes (the ‘tilted batch only’ variant omits the reference-batch estimate); all other terms are evaluated under ℙ \mathbb{P} on the reference batch. The controllers minimise Eq. 85 with λ KL = 10 − 4 \lambda_{\KL}=10^{-4} , a 6 6 -nat wall, target log-weights clipped at ± 5 \pm 5 and Adam with learning rate 2 ⋅ 10 − 3 2\cdot 10^{-3} on their own parameters; the backbone keeps the optimiser and schedule of the vanilla runs. The tilt studies use seven seeds and 1 000 1\,000 epochs; the tilted arms cost 1.3 × 1.3\times the epoch time of the budget-matched untilted arm ( 303 303 against 229 229 ms).

sections.heading: The tilt as a learned importance sampler: protocol.
sections.text: To isolate the benefit of the tilt from the calibration task, we evaluate it on toy in a controlled estimator study against ordinary Monte Carlo at the same compute budget. The reference law is the three-layer toy cell of Table 2 , simulated at N = 512 N=512 steps with ρ = 0 \rho=0 and calibrated seven times with different seeds. The targets are the exceedance probabilities ℙ ⁡ ( Y T > H ) \mathbb{P}(Y_{T}>H) with H H at the model’s own quantiles of nominal probability 10 − 2 10^{-2} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 10 − 4 10^{-4} ; reference values come from 8 × 10 5 8\times 10^{5} plain Monte-Carlo paths. For each backbone one controller per threshold is trained post hoc, in three stages of 1 000 1\,000 cross-entropy steps on batches of 1 024 1\,024 tilted paths, the stage for the rarer event starting from the controller of the previous one, under the wall κ = − log ⁡ p + 2 \kappa=-\log p+2 nats. Every estimator receives the same per-estimate path budget n n ; in addition, plain Monte Carlo receives a cost-matched budget inflated by the measured per-path overhead of the tilted simulation (a factor 1.18 1.18 ). The relative root-mean-square error of every estimator is measured over 100 100 independent replications, and the tables report the mean and standard error over the seven backbones.

sections.text: The wall κ \kappa in Eq. 85 controls how far the Girsanov proposal may move from the reference measure, and the choice of controller objective decides whether it moves at all.
